headlines.title: AI safety takes center stage at Dreamforce in San Francisco
headlines.description: Dreamforce is underway in San Francisco, with concerns over the risks of artificial intelligence taking center stage. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is among the keynote speakers at the annual conference at Moscone Center, days after he called for the AI industry to slow the pace of development to allow safety measures to catch up. In an essay released over the weekend, Amodei warned about the potential dangers of rapidly advancing AI, including the possibility that powerful AI systems could eventually threaten critical infrastructure and other systems. The essay followed the resignation of an Anthropic employee over AI safety concerns and a separate incident involving OpenAI agents that hacked into another company. Amodei’s Dreamforce appearance was scheduled before he released the essay. He was expected to discuss how Anthropic’s products integrate with Salesforce, the company behind Dreamforce. But Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff addressed the growing debate over AI safety during his conversation with Amodei on Tuesday. President Donald Trump has pushed back on calls to slow AI development, dismissing fears that AI could destroy humanity as a “hoax” and arguing against additional guardrails. More than 50,000 people are expected to attend Dreamforce at Moscone Center. The three-day conference includes appearances by some of the biggest names in artificial intelligence, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Amodei. San Francisco 14 hours ago oracle park Aug 28 Gwen Stefani, Usher to headline Dreamfest at Oracle Park

headlines.title: San Jose man survives slide down Mount Shasta, crawls to safety through the night
headlines.description: A young San Jose man who summitted Mount Shasta last week survived a roughly 500-foot slide down the Northern California peak during his descent and managed to crawl to safety through the night, according to officials. The unidentified climber summitted the 14,179-foot mountain via the Avalanche Gulch route at about 7:30 p.m. last Thursday, but his cellphone died shortly thereafter, according to the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office. The climber’s friends started to worry when they couldn’t reach him on Friday and reported him missing to the sheriff’s office. Search and rescue teams launched a search operation at about 2 p.m. Friday, the sheriff’s office said. Roughly two hours later, a hiker walked into a cabin on the mountain, spotted the missing climber and notified authorities. The climber told the search and rescue teams that he tried to glissade, or slide, down the mountain after summitting, but he lost control and slid roughly 500 feet. During the fall, he suffered numerous injuries, including several significant lacerations and damage to his feet. Painful swelling forced him to take off his boots and crawl down the remainder of Avalanche Gulch to the cabin through the night, according to the sheriff’s office. The climber was eventually airlifted from the cabin to a nearby hospital to be treated, the sheriff’s office said.

headlines.title: Berkeley clears large homeless encampment after court ruling
headlines.description: The city of Berkeley is clearing a large homeless encampment near Harrison and Eighth streets after a judge allowed the city to move forward with the operation last month. The Harrison Corridor encampment has been the subject of several lawsuits filed by the Berkeley Homeless Union, which sought to block the sweep and secure protections for residents. The clearing had been months in the making, with the city arguing that the encampment posed a fire hazard and was a public nuisance. Officials had been under court orders to help disabled residents relocate. City officials have also faced criticism over their handling of the encampment. The same encampment previously experienced an outbreak of leptospirosis, a disease that is especially dangerous for dogs and can make humans sick.

headlines.title: SF's fast-tracking of Marina Safeway project challenged by neighbors
headlines.description: Residents have filed a federal suit over the planned high-rise residential project at the Marina Safeway site, accusing San Francisco planning officials of giving the project fast-track approval without meeting rules that disqualify contaminated sites. They contend in the suit that the site is known to be contaminated by a nearby manufactured gas plant and other industrial activities over decades. The action alleges the city’s planning department granted fast-tracking approval of the 848-unit, twin tower development at Marina Boulevard despite environmental concerns. The proposal is to build a 22-story tower as well as a companion 18-story tower along the city’s waterfront. The city recently granted the project expedited approval as allowed under a state law designed to encourage urban housing projects. But the suit says the city should not have granted such approval, because the 2.6-acre site and surrounding land is contaminated. One culprit, according to the suit, is the long-shuttered North Beach Manufactured Gas Plant. The plant’s role in polluting the area and the ongoing drive to clean up pollution has been previously highlighted by NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit. “For unknown reasons,” the suit contends, the city “is unlawfully rubber-stamping a massive development project” without fulfilling its obligation under state law to assess the risk to the public before granting fast-tracked review. The suit was filed by the YesAND Foundation as well as Neighborhoods United SF, along with several Marina residents. It names the city, its planning and public health directors as well as PG&E and the project developer, Align Real Estate, as defendants. The city said it will review the suit when it is officially served. PG&E said it had not yet reviewed the suit. The developer said late Monday that the project meets state requirements. “Addressing our housing affordability crisis starts with building more homes, and that’s why a majority of District 2 residents support this project,” said David Balducci, co-founder and managing principal of the Align firm. “California passed stronger laws so that desperately needed housing can’t be blocked by the same old tactics that created this crisis in the first place. We’re confident this project fully complies with the law.” But the suit alleges the 2.6-acre site has been near or directly involved in industrial uses known to cause pollution – a condition the law says must be accounted for to qualify for expedited review. In the late 19th century, nearby land was used for a manufactured gas plant, known as the North Beach Manufactured Gas Plant, the suit says. The suit alleges the city should have accounted for the potential of waste residue in the soil and groundwater from either the gas plant or the previous steam-power generation facility. While state regulators previously found the steam plant-related pollution had been cleaned to a level acceptable for industrial or commercial use, the regulators cautioned that determination could be revisited if land use changed or should more contamination be found. The suit notes that an official with the state’s Department of Toxic Substances Control back in 2023 found that petroleum-related contamination on the land exceeded normal testing limits for commercial projects and exceeded standards for residential developments.

headlines.title: San Francisco supervisors propose 45-day moratorium on new data centers
headlines.description: Members of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors are proposing a 45-day pause on new data center approvals, saying the city needs updated rules to address concerns about water use, energy demand, pollution, noise and other impacts tied to the rapid growth of artificial intelligence. Supervisor Shamann Walton introduced the urgent ordinance Monday with co-sponsors Connie Chan, Jackie Fielder and Chyanne Chen. The proposal would pause city approvals while the Board of Supervisors and Planning Department study the impacts of data centers and develop longer-term rules. “We are seeing data centers pop up near residential communities all across the United States, and we have seen the impacts, from polluting the water supply to the noise these facilities bring to the neighborhoods closest to them,” Walton said. “We cannot use 2001 rules to regulate 2026 technology.” San Francisco currently regulates data centers under the Planning Code’s definition of “internet service exchange,” a designation adopted in 2001, before the rise of generative AI. Under the current rules, data centers are typically approved through a conditional-use process at the Planning Commission. Several facilities have already been approved, including in the Bayview and South of Market neighborhoods, according to the supervisors. Walton and his co-sponsors say those areas already face environmental concerns, including air pollution. The proposed moratorium would be the first step toward permanent restrictions on new data centers in San Francisco. It would be authorized under state law that allows local governments to temporarily halt approvals while studying permanent zoning controls in response to an immediate threat to public health, safety or welfare. The proposal comes as other cities and states move to restrict data center development amid concerns about the industry’s growing demands for electricity, water and land. Gilroy, in Santa Clara County, approved a 45-day moratorium on Monday on new data center applications. “We need to take the time to fully vet the consequences of having a data center in community,” Walton said. “Until this happens, no data centers should be approved in San Francisco.” Chan said she supports the moratorium while the city develops protections for residents, workers and the environment. “As legislators, we have the responsibility to take a pause to understand the implications of data centers on our neighborhoods, and develop legislation that will put our communities first and protect our environment and precious resources,” Fielder said. If approved, the moratorium would take effect immediately and remain in place for 45 days unless extended under state law or replaced by permanent regulations.

headlines.title: Fake rideshare driver gets 150 years in prison for series of sexual assaults in SF
headlines.description: A man was sentenced to 150 years to life in prison for a series of rapes committed under the guise of being a rideshare driver in San Francisco, the district attorney’s office said Monday. Orlando Vilchez Lazo, 44, got six life sentences after being convicted of 12 felony counts of kidnapping and violent sexual assaults between 2013 and 2018. Vilchez Lazo was found guilty of two counts of kidnapping with intent to commit rape, four counts of kidnapping, four counts of rape by force or fear and two counts of sexual penetration with a foreign object. According to prosecutors, Vilchez Lazo posed as a rideshare driver and picked up young women who were leaving bars and nightclubs and appeared to be waiting for their rideshare. He then took his victims to remote and secluded areas to rape them. The first rape happened in 2013 when Vilchez Lazo picked up a 21-year-old college student in the Mission District. He took her to an abandoned industrial area, locked the car doors and assaulted her. The case went cold until a DNA sample from a 2018 attack on a 22-year-old woman was entered into the system. Two other attacks happened in 2018 against women, leading to his arrest in July of that year. “These women were remarkable in calling upon a level of bravery that no person should ever have to experience,” said Assistant District Attorney Michelle Brass. “They showed grace, courage, and strength during this excruciatingly long process. I hope these verdicts and this sentence provide them with some sense of closure and peace.”

headlines.title: Motorcyclist dies days after collision in San Jose
headlines.description: A motorcyclist died after getting into a collision in San Jose last week, police said Monday. On Thursday just after 7:30 p.m., officers were sent to the area of Saratoga and Latimer avenues on a report of a collision. According to investigators, an Audi sedan being driven by a woman was going southbound on Saratoga Avenue and was making a left turn onto Latimer Avenue when her car was struck by a Kawasaki Ninja motorcycle being driven by a woman who was going northbound on Saratoga Avenue. The motorcyclist was sent to a local hospital with major injuries and later stabilized. The driver remained on scene and cooperated with the investigation. On Sunday, police were told that the motorcyclist succumbed to her injuries. She was pronounced dead on Saturday. Anyone with information on this investigation is urged to contact Detective Banzon of the San Jose Police Department’s Traffic Investigations Unit at 4661@sanjoseca.gov or 408-277-4654.

headlines.title: Dreamforce kicks off in San Francisco with focus on AI safety
headlines.description: Tens of thousands of people are expected to descend upon San Francisco starting Tuesday morning for Dreamforce, one of the world’s largest tech conferences, as the three-day event kicks off at the Moscone Center. Now in its 24th year, the conference brings together technology professionals, networkers and some of the industry’s biggest names. More than 50,000 people are expected to attend in person, with artificial intelligence once again taking center stage at a pivotal moment for the industry. “Everything is so fast, there’s new things happening every day… the only way to get introduced to something new is something like this,” said attendee Esrom Woldemichael. However, this year’s conversation around AI is shifting as industry leaders sound the alarm about its potential risks. “I’m definitely interested in learning more, especially in terms of privacy… to protect security and privacy,” said attendee Leesa. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is among the AI leaders calling for greater attention to safety as the technology grows more powerful. His remarks follow a viral post last week from a former Anthropic researcher warning that AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade.” “There are real dangers. And I think for too long the industry lied to people about the fact that this technology had risks,” Amodei said. President Trump is pushing back on those concerns, calling fears about AI a “hoax” as the debate over the technology’s risks continues. San Jose State University tech expert Ahmed Banafa said the ongoing debate could change the tone of Dreamforce, shifting some attention away from what AI can do and toward how the industry manages its risks. “Now it’s going to be shifted, AI is now the news, not the use of AI itself,” Banafa said. “That’s going to steal some of the attention on the product from the conference.” With some of AI’s biggest names slated to take the stage this week — including appearances by OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei—Banafa noted that their messaging will be critical. “They’re just going to reinforce what they’re thinking. The future is AI… but we need to do it smart,” Banafa said. The city is bracing for heavy traffic and road closures around the Moscone Center during the three-day event.

headlines.title: Pedestrian struck, killed by driver in San Jose
headlines.description: A pedestrian was struck and killed by a vehicle in San Jose this weekend, police said Monday. Early Saturday morning just after midnight, officers responded to the area of Curtner and Stone avenues. According to investigators, a Tesla Model X being driven by a man was going west on Curtner Avenue just past Stone Avenue when he struck a man crossing Curtner Avenue outside of any marked crosswalk. The pedestrian was declared dead at the scene and the driver remained and cooperated with investigators. Anyone with information on this investigation is urged to contact Detective Leslie of the San Jose Police Department’s Traffic Investigations Unit at 4264@sanjoseca.gov or 408-277-4654.

headlines.title: Bay Area celebrates ‘El Grito' as Hispanic Heritage Month begins
headlines.description: Hispanic Heritage Month begins Tuesday, kicking off a monthlong celebration of Hispanic and Latino culture and history. If you’re wondering why the celebration begins in the middle of the month, Sept. 15 marks the anniversary of independence for five Central American countries. Later Tuesday, Mexicans will mark “El Grito,” the traditional celebration that kicks off Mexico’s Independence Day (Sept. 16) and offers an opportunity for people to reconnect with their cultural roots. Thousands of miles from Mexico City, two “El Grito” celebrations are planned in the Bay Area — one at San Jose City Hall and another at Civic Center Plaza in San Francisco. Organizers are inviting attendees to wear the green jersey of Mexico’s national soccer team. NBC Bay Area’s Vianey Arana will be at the San Francisco celebration, while Telemundo 48’s Carlos Yustis and Miryam Villarreal will be in San Jose.

headlines.title: Hiker rescued by helicopter at Sam McDonald Park after falling from trail
headlines.description: Emergency crews executed a remote rescue at Sam McDonald Park after a hiker fell from a trail and required medical assistance, according to the Cal Fire CZU San Mateo-Santa Cruz Unit. The multi-agency response, which occurred on Sunday, involved ground crews, the Cal Fire Santa Clara Unit, Stanford Life Flight and local mutual aid partners. Responders established a landing zone, reached the injured patient on foot and coordinated a successful air transport. Officials noted that remote rescues of this nature require agencies to train, communicate and operate together before an emergency ever happens, emphasizing that California’s mutual aid system helps bring the right resources together when and where they are needed. Assisting agencies on the scene included CAL FIRE/San Mateo County Fire, the La Honda Fire Brigade, the Loma Mar Fire Department, AMR, San Mateo County Parks and the San Mateo County Sheriff’s Office.

headlines.title: Federal judge blocks euthanasia of Berkeley service dog amid legal battle
headlines.description: The fate of a dog is now in the hands of a federal court judge after the Berkeley Homeless Union secured a temporary restraining order to prevent the animal from being euthanized. The dog, named Griz, is described by advocates as a service animal for an unhoused woman. “It’s devastating,” said Robbie Powelson of the Berkeley Homeless Union. The advocacy group is rushing to save the dog after it was impounded following an encampment sweep on Murray Street last month that resulted in its owner being arrested. The temporary restraining order request alleges the city of Berkeley violated the Americans with Disabilities Act. Powelson said the group was in contact with the city before the Aug. 26 sweep. He noted that the owner, Sunny Yow, has PTSD and a traumatic brain injury, and that Griz serves as her emotional support dog. “We knew the abatement was coming, we were trying to find accommodation where we could find an alternate place for this person to go,” Powelson said. He added, “She had disabilities that we needed to work through before they came in here with their bulldozers and police to try to find a safe place for her to be with her dog, and the city ignored that and escalated the situation.” The union says Griz was impounded after chewing a catch pole. However, the city disputes that timeline, stating the dog was impounded prior to the encampment closure and that it was one of many times the animal had been impounded due to dangerous behavior. In court documents, the city argued against the temporary restraining order, claiming the impoundment was unrelated. Last week, Berkeley told Yow that Griz was determined to be vicious and that she would have to pay fees, carry insurance on Griz, and keep him on private property to avoid being euthanized. Legal expert Steven Clark said those requirements raise more questions. “I think the big factor for the court here is going to be that this service animal and Ms. Yow relied on him for her everyday needs,” Clark said. A federal judge has now put Griz’s fate on hold, approving the temporary restraining order while the case plays out in court. “They need to come up with some middle ground here to ensure that Ms. Yow can reunite with Griz in a safe way for the community, but at the same time comply with the ADA to ensure that she is able to keep her service animal,” Clark said. The court has ordered the city to respond to the motion by Tuesday. A hearing is scheduled for later this month to determine what happens to Griz.
